preservation.upstream_action: When deciding whether to continue, look only at future input and future return, not at how much was already invested.
Accept that the time already invested is gone and cannot be recovered (cost: no money).
Count only how much more must still be invested and how much can still be gotten back.
Do not count what has already been spent.
Benefit claim: avoiding the tendency means you will not keep investing time just because you do not want to waste what you put in.
Remark: the Arkes and Blumer theatre ticket experiment (per-group visit counts) and the Roth finding that the effect fades with time and is weaker in older adults.

findings.text: Oddziel nieodwracalny wydatek od tego, co nadal możesz odzyskać lub wykorzystać.
findings.why: The upstream rule has two steps: count only the future outlay and the future return, and leave out what is already spent. The item's two sentences never say to leave the irreversible part out of the comparison: 'Oddziel' only separates it. The worked question names only the cost side (one evening) and does not prompt the reader to estimate the expected future return. Both halves of the rule survive only through the title. A reader acting on W praktyce alone may separate the sunk amount and still weigh it.

findings.text: B — badanie pierwotne i przegląd potwierdzają błąd decyzyjny, ale nie mierzą korzyści z tej konkretnej instrukcji.
findings.why: The letter B is consistent with the README B row (review without one common effect size): the Roth abstract says the effect size is contingent on decision type and reports no pooled estimate. The justification does not use that reason. It rests partly on a primary study that was not read (see the limitations finding). Elsewhere the item calls the Roth work 'Przegląd', although the abstract describes a quantitative meta-analysis of 98 effect sizes, which AGENTS.md says to call a synthesis. The letter does not hide low certainty, so this is wording only.
